So with no further ado, here's our show on lessons in growth equity investing with Volition

Yeah, I think it's when you kind of have clear line of sight. And I'm speaking about series A,

hey, a dollar ends going to get me more than a dollar out. And I'm ready to scale and build

of the team. So I think a lot of them, the management team is wearing a lot of hats. So

think that one thing that we kind of left about that's somewhat funny and somewhat not funny is
that, you know, our investments typical whole period may be five or seven to seven years in the U.S.
that's longer than the average marriage last statistically. So you need to know the person
that you're going to be working with. I am cognizant that there are a lot of other growth equity funds

to our initial conversation. If they're telling you, hey, we expect a hundred X return, but you

And then the last one I'd say is how they interact with their portfolio companies. So
if you think about like a family office, they're going to be a little bit different than an
institutional investor. A family office tends to be more passive capital where Volition, on the
other hand, we hold a minority equity position in our company. So we're not like in the weeds

someone who might be more just passive capital. And can you drill down a little bit more into
why it's so important to your investment thesis to invest into founder-led companies where they're
still maintaining a material ownership and not getting rid of the vast majority of their equity
stake? Yeah, I mean, I think it just aligns us where from an investment perspective, I'm not
making a lot of money unless the founders make a lot of money. And I've seen scenarios in other
companies where maybe a founder gets deluded over time. They own single digit percentage of the
business and things aren't going the way that everyone expected. And they're like, life's too
short. I have another idea. I'm going to go try and try my hand at that. And then the business is
out to CEOs. So however, if someone still owns a good portion of the business, even if it's
challenging time, they're still aligned to try to drive it to an exit. Because if you want to go
a portion and maybe things don't go exactly the way you thought, but you can still drive a decent
exit, you're still going to walk away with a good amount of money from a returns perspective.
So I think that aligns us. And then part of the reason why we like many times to be the first
capital in, or at least aligned with the other investors in the cap table is time horizon and
how people think about returns. And I've also seen scenarios where you have two investors,
one that could end in a very different price, and they'd be happy at an exit that might be
only a 2x return for the next investor. And that causes a little bit of conflict at the board.
And maybe someone wants to get liquidity because they want to show a realized return because they're
now raising another fund. You've got to take all that into consideration when you think about
people's exit timeline horizons. Yeah, there's a sure a lot of dynamics to think about. And one
that I find pretty fascinating is balancing alignment and incentives. In addition, from
the institutional capital provider's perspective, perhaps some downside protection. You hear
some of the structuring on some of these investments, whether they're preferred shares,
liquidity preference, those sort of features where I've heard some kind of nightmarish type
stories where it appears there's a big exit, but nothing for the founders just given how the
investments were structured in liquidity preference. How do you think about balancing that dynamic?
Yeah, I mean, I think industry standard for a Series A or Series B institutional investment is
like a bare minimum. You have your buying preferred shares in a 1x liquidation preference.
That is kind of table stakes. And you could say that's misaligned or not, but that's the
reality of the situation. However, most of the time in those scenarios, if the investor is the
only one that's going to get paid, there's no incentive to management to continue. So there
tends to be a management carve out to make sure that people are not walking away with nothing.
But part of the reason that you have that is like, let's say a growth equity fund invested 20
million, things don't go the way that people had hoped. And the business winds up selling for 15
million. In theory, in a 1x liquidation preference, the investor would get the first 20 million out
of the business to make sure that they get their money back. Part of the reason for that is if
they didn't have that and they own whatever 25% of the business, the founders can still walk away
with $5 million each and they're happy. That's still a lot of money for them. And the investors
is in the red. They didn't make any money. So that's where I actually think that it is trying to
drive alignment at the end of the day because the investor is not playing with house money.
They're putting actual money in where the founder may be kind of sweat equity where
it's just their time. And that's where it does get back to alignment a little bit.
Right. And one of the main drivers of the thesis behind some of your investments is this product
market fit. Now, how do you think about that dynamic, like true product market fit versus
just good near-term sales momentum? Or how do you think about it in terms of total addressable
market? It's a great question, especially with how fast we've seen businesses scale with AI.
I think for whatever reason, the arbitrary number that a lot of series A growth equity
funds have decided on product market fit is $5 million run rate. You can almost kind of grit
your way there if you have a decent product and then you need to start building the infrastructure
that we've talked about to set yourself up for future scale. And historically, I think if you're
an enterprise B2B SaaS company, for example, it might take two years or so to get to a $5
million run rate because you're building the product and you got to have 20 to 30 employees
based on just a number of engineers and sales reps and customer success and so forth that you have.
So there's more of a time horizon of 24 months or so for us as investors to analyze.
In AI world, like we've seen businesses go zero to 20 million run rate in nine months now, which
was like truly unheard of before. And maybe all of those customers haven't even been up for renewal
yet. So you don't even know what the retention is going to look like. So that's where you are
taking a little bit of a bet and it's a different diligence process. But part of it is trying to
understand stuff like usage patterns, how critical is this to people's day to day workflows.
We always do customer reference calls. Like all those customer reference calls, you really got
to figure out are people, is this mission critical or a nice to have, which could be an indicator
for churn later down the line. And I think everyone is trying to figure that out because
these companies can scale so fast with so few people now because of the development cycles

human capital oriented with Asians. So we're in a new era of defining what product market fit looks

for the first renewal and it's a mass tournament. And luckily we haven't invested in any of those,

how are people actually using and interacting and what are the usage patterns of the business.
Yeah, and with respect to AI, there's just so much potential and as you indicated risk, you hear

Yeah, one that has less influence there. Yes.
Yeah, it's interesting. So our fund, we've never been pure play software investors or tech

company public. So you really got to feel like there is like a huge opportunity to kind of ride

event for the investor right away. Right. And another segment of the market that has grown is

markets? Do you participate either from either an entrance or exit perspective?
Yeah, it's funny. Something that we've gotten a lot more comfortable with as our fund size got a
little bit bigger, I'd say a decent portion of our investments have some level of liquidity

freeze them up to potentially accelerate growth. So yeah, we've definitely gotten comfortable
